Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette:
At seventy-six, Eleanor Vance believed she had seen everything the sea could throw at a person. As captain of a container ship, she had navigated hurricanes, equipment failures, and the complex politics of international ports with a steady hand. She was a woman defined by her competence and control. The trauma that unmoored her, however, did not happen on the water. It happened six months ago on a sun-drenched city plaza, where she had gone to support her granddaughter at a peaceful climate protest. She remembered the sudden shift in the crowd, the line of police in riot gear. The event itself remained not as a continuous film but as a series of shockingly clear and detailed still frames. When she remembered what happened, it was just like looking at photographs in her mind: the glint of a visor, the raised baton, the panicked face of a young man beside her, and then the hard, unforgiving grey of the pavement rushing up to meet her as she was shoved from behind.

In the weeks that followed, these mental photographs began to intrude at unwelcome moments. Standing on the bridge, the glint of sunlight off the water would suddenly become the glint of that helmet visor. The sharp clang of a dropped tool on the deck would echo the sound of batons on shields. During these moments, the memory was so powerful that she felt like it was happening right now; she could feel the phantom ache in her shoulder and the cold shock of the ground. To escape these vivid intrusions, Eleanor threw herself into her work with a ferocity that worried her first mate. She would stay on the bridge for sixteen-hour stretches, keeping her mind occupied with the familiar calculus of currents and tides. She took over inventory checks, engine room logs—any task that demanded her full attention and left no room for the images to surface. The ship, once her domain, became her hiding place.

This strategy of overworking, however, only offered temporary relief and, perversely, seemed to strengthen the memories' hold on her. The exhaustion she courted during the day left her defenseless in the crushing quiet of her cabin at night. Sleep offered no escape. Lying in her bunk, her mind, too tired to fend off the thoughts, would begin its relentless inquiry. She would go over and over why the event had happened to her, a woman who had always followed the rules, trying to find a logic that wasn't there. This rumination only seemed to etch the images of that day more deeply into her mind, making them clearer and more detailed with each passing week. The more she tried to make sense of the chaos, the more she felt she was reliving it.

The cycle tightened its grip over the months. A photographic memory would flash into her mind on the bridge, and in response, she would bury herself in work until she was numb with fatigue. That night, the exhaustion would give way to hours of dwelling on the captain she used to be before the event—calm, decisive, unafraid. This painful contrast between her past and present self would make the memories feel even more potent and devastating when they inevitably returned the next day. Her crew began to notice the change, the new tension in her posture, the way she would flinch at sudden noises. She had become a stranger on her own ship, haunted by images of dry land. It was after she misread a weather report, a simple mistake born of sheer mental fatigue that could have had serious consequences, that Eleanor knew she could no longer manage alone. The fear of her own mind making her a danger on the water, of losing the one part of her life that still felt like her own, was what finally brought her ashore to seek help.
